title: Remote Service Session Hijacking
summary: Remote service session hijacking is lateral movement that takes over a session which is already open instead of creating a new one. When a user logs into a remote service such as Secure Shell (SSH), Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), or telnet, the service creates a session object that represents that authenticated interaction, and the session carries the user's identity and permissions for as long as it lives. An adversary who already holds sufficient rights on the host can attach to that session and issue commands inside it, which means no new authentication takes place and no credential is presented. The detection consequence is significant: because there is no fresh logon, indicators built around failed or unusual authentication simply do not fire, and account based anomaly detection sees the legitimate user doing what they normally do. What does change is session state and process ownership. Session identifiers stay the same while the controlling connection or client changes, processes are launched under a session whose interactive owner is elsewhere, and in some cases the original user is disconnected or loses access without explanation. Platforms differ in mechanism, which is why the specific sub-techniques matter: SSH relies on the agent and its keys, while RDP relies on session handling and permissions in the terminal services layer. The practical defensive approach is behavioural: baseline how reconnection tools are used, watch session state changes, and correlate process activity with the session identifier it belongs to.

beginner.definition: A remote session is a live connection between two computers, such as a remote desktop or a secure command line. This technique is about an attacker taking over a session that someone else already opened. They do not log in with a stolen password and they do not create a new connection. They simply step into the existing one. It belongs to the group of techniques used to move between machines.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most detection watches for strange logins, wrong passwords, or new connections. A hijacked session produces none of those, because the login already happened and the user is real. The attacker inherits whatever that session was allowed to do, which may include administrative rights. The real user might be disconnected or never notice anything unusual. This makes session hijacking a quiet way to reach machines that are hard to access directly.
howItWorks: A real user opens a remote session, such as a remote desktop or secure shell connection.
That session stays alive while the user works, holding their identity and their rights.
The attacker gains high level access on the same machine, or on a trusted machine.
They attach to the existing session or borrow the credentials it already holds.
Their commands run as that user, so no new login or password check takes place.
Defenders look for session state changes, odd process ownership, and reconnection events.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel room that a guest has already unlocked with their own key card. A cleaner with a master card enters the room and uses the guest's desk phone, minibar, and room service account. Every purchase appears on the guest's bill and nothing at reception shows a new check in. The room was never broken into, it was simply used by someone else.
takeaways: Hijacking reuses a live session, so no new authentication event appears in logs.
The attacker inherits the permissions of the session they take over.
Detection focuses on session state changes and which session runs each process.

objectives: Define remote service session hijacking and contrast it with creating a new remote session.
Explain why hijacking produces no new authentication event and what that means for detection.
Describe which session attributes change and which stay the same during a hijack.
Name the platforms and services where session hijacking is most commonly observed.
Identify log sources that record session reconnection and disconnect activity.
Outline controls such as limiting idle sessions and reducing standing administrative rights.
